questions.question_text: A 68-year-old male with chronic stable angina and resting heart rate of 88 bpm is prescribed ivabradine. Which phase of the sinoatrial nodal action potential does this medication selectively inhibit?
questions.clinical_vignette: The patient has moderate systolic heart failure and cannot tolerate further uptitration of beta-adrenergic antagonists due to symptomatic hypotension and reactive airway disease.

questions.question_text: In an isolated canine cardiac muscle experiment, increasing the initial resting length of ventricular sarcomeres from 1.8 µm to 2.2 µm produces a marked increase in active tension generation. Which molecular mechanism primarily accounts for this phenomenon?
questions.clinical_vignette: This physiological property forms the primary biological basis of the Frank-Starling law of the heart.

questions.question_text: A 54-year-old woman receiving oral sotalol for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with syncope. Telemetry reveals runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with twisting of the QRS complexes around the isoelectric line. What is the fundamental electrophysiologic trigger responsible for this arrhythmia?
questions.clinical_vignette: Her baseline 12-lead ECG demonstrates a corrected QT (QTc) interval of 560 ms. Serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L and magnesium is 1.4 mg/dL.

questions.question_text: An autopsy is conducted on a 62-year-old man who succumbed to sudden cardiogenic shock 4 days after an acute anterior wall myocardial infarction. Histological examination of the infarcted myocardium is most likely to demonstrate which of the following findings?
questions.clinical_vignette: Post-mortem examination reveals transmural myocardial infarction in the distribution of the left anterior descending coronary artery.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after an unintentional opioid overdose. Arterial blood gas on room air shows: pH 7.24, PaCO2 62 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg, HCO3- 26 mEq/L. Assuming a respiratory quotient of 0.8, which statement best characterizes his alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient?
questions.clinical_vignette: Patient has pinpoint pupils and shallow breathing at 6 breaths per minute. He has no prior cardiopulmonary medical history.

questions.question_text: A 19-year-old female with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul respirations. Laboratory evaluation reveals: Na+ 132 mEq/L, K+ 5.4 mEq/L, Cl- 94 mEq/L, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, Glucose 480 mg/dL. What is her serum anion gap, and what is the primary pathophysiologic cause?
questions.clinical_vignette: Urinalysis reveals 4+ ketones and 3+ glucose. Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is markedly elevated.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antiarrhythmic agents carries the highest risk of QTc prolongation through block of rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr), while paradoxically maintaining a relatively low clinical incidence of Torsades de Pointes?
questions.clinical_vignette: The drug possesses mixed Class I, II, III, and IV electrophysiological properties and has extensive tissue accumulation with a half-life of 40-55 days.

answer_choices.choice_text: Phase 0 rapid sodium influx through voltage-gated Nav1.5 channels
Phase 4 spontaneous slow diastolic depolarization mediated by funny (If) inward mixed Na+/K+ currents
Phase 2 plateau maintained by L-type calcium channel activation
Phase 3 rapid repolarization through delayed rectifier potassium channels
Increased sensitivity of troponin C to intracellular Ca2+ and optimal actin-myosin overlap geometry
Phosphorylation of phospholamban by cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase A
Enhanced extracellular sodium efflux via the 3Na+/2K+ ATPase pump
Direct opening of ryanodine receptors independent of transsarcolemmal calcium influx
Delayed afterdepolarizations (DADs) triggered by intracellular calcium overload in Phase 4
Early afterdepolarizations (EADs) occurring during prolonged Phase 2 or Phase 3 repolarization
Anatomical reentry circuit around an infarcted myocardial scar border zone
Loss of vagal efferent transmission at the atrioventricular junction
Wavy myocardial fibers with contraction band necrosis and early edema without cellular infiltrate
Dense neutrophil infiltration with extensive karyorrhexis and early macrophage-mediated disintegration of necrotic myocytes
Established dense hypocellular collagen scar with extensive neovascular capillary regression
Granulation tissue with abundant proliferating capillary loops and active myofibroblast collagen deposition
Normal A-a gradient (~5 to 10 mmHg), confirming pure alveolar hypoventilation as the sole cause of hypoxemia
Elevated A-a gradient (>35 mmHg), indicating acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Elevated A-a gradient (>25 mmHg), indicating acute pulmonary embolism with ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Markedly depressed A-a gradient (<0 mmHg), indicating severe diffusion barrier impairment

Anion gap = 28 mEq/L (High anion gap metabolic acidosis secondary to unmeasured ketoacid anions: acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate)
Anion gap = 38 mEq/L (High anion gap acidosis secondary to severe hyperchloremic expansion)
Anion gap = 8 mEq/L (Low anion gap acidosis due to hypoalbuminemia)

explanations.explanation_text: CORRECT: Ivabradine acts specifically on the hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels in the SA node. By selectively blocking the inward mixed Na+/K+ funny current (If) during Phase 4 slow diastolic depolarization, ivabradine decreases the slope of Phase 4 and slows heart rate without exerting negative inotropic or vasodilatory actions.
explanations.source_document: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 28: Pharmacotherapy of Congestive Heart Failure

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Phase 0 in SA nodal pacemaker cells is mediated by inward calcium flow through L-type Ca2+ channels (Cav1.2), not fast voltage-gated Nav1.5 channels (which are absent or inactivated in nodal tissue). Class I antiarrhythmics block Nav1.5 in working ventricular myocytes.
explanations.source_document: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 10: Rhythmical Excitation of the Heart

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Phase 2 plateau is prominent in working ventricular and atrial myocytes, not SA pacemaker cells which have no sustained plateau phase. Dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers inhibit L-type calcium channels.
explanations.source_document: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 9: Cardiac Muscle; The Heart as a Pump

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Phase 3 repolarization in the SA node is carried by outward delayed rectifier potassium currents (IKr, IKs). Class III antiarrhythmic agents block these channels, prolonging action potential duration.
explanations.source_document: Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 14: Agents Used in Cardiac Arrhythmias

explanations.explanation_text: CORRECT: The Frank-Starling mechanism relies on length-dependent activation of cardiac muscle. As end-diastolic sarcomere length increases toward the optimal length (~2.2 µm), reduced interfilament lattice spacing enhances cross-bridge formation and increases the affinity of troponin C for ionized calcium, producing greater contractile tension at any given cytosolic [Ca2+].
explanations.source_document: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, 3rd Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 22: The Heart as a Pump; Frank-Starling Law

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Phospholamban phosphorylation by PKA occurs upon beta-1 adrenergic stimulation (positive inotropy/lusitropy) and disinhibits SERCA2a, accelerating calcium re-uptake. It is not the baseline mechanism of length-dependent passive stretch.
explanations.source_document: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, 3rd Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 22: Autonomic Regulation of Cardiac Performance

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: The Na+/K+ ATPase maintains transmembrane resting electrochemical gradients. Inhibition (e.g. by digoxin), rather than increased efflux, raises intracellular Na+ and indirectly drives Ca2+ accumulation via NCX reverse mode.
explanations.source_document: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 4: Transport of Substances Through Cell Membranes

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Ryanodine receptor (RyR2) activation in cardiac myocytes is strictly dependent on calcium-induced calcium release (CICR) triggered by transsarcolemmal Ca2+ influx through L-type channels.
explanations.source_document: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 9: Excitation-Contraction Coupling in Cardiac Muscle

explanations.explanation_text: CORRECT: Sotalol blocks the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr), causing marked prolongation of myocardial repolarization (prolonged QT interval). When repolarization is excessively delayed, voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels can recover from inactivation, precipitating early afterdepolarizations (EADs). If an EAD reaches threshold during the relative refractory period, it initiates Torsades de Pointes.
explanations.source_document: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine, 12th Ed
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 42: Mechanisms of Cardiac Arrhythmias

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Delayed afterdepolarizations (DADs) occur after complete repolarization during Phase 4 and are driven by sarcoplasmic reticulum spontaneous calcium release causing transient inward currents (Iti). DADs are classic for digoxin toxicity, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, and hypercalcemia.
explanations.source_document: Braunwald's Heart Disease, 12th Ed
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 42: Triggered Activity & DADs

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Fixed anatomic reentry around scar tissue produces monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with uniform QRS morphology, not polymorphic Torsades de Pointes characterized by undulation of QRS axes.
explanations.source_document: Braunwald's Heart Disease, 12th Ed
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 43: Ventricular Tachyarrhythmias

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Vagal loss would increase sinus node automaticity and AV nodal conduction velocity, but does not generate EAD-mediated polymorphic ventricular dysrhythmias.
explanations.source_document: The explanation is not available in the provided source files.
explanations.source_reference: Reference not cited

explanations.explanation_text: CORRECT: At day 3 to 7 post-MI, microscopic inspection reveals dense neutrophilic infiltration undergoing apoptosis/karyorrhexis, with active phagocytosis of dead necrotic myocytes by incoming mononuclear macrophages. The necrotic muscle tissue is markedly softened, explaining why mechanical complications (such as ventricular free wall rupture, ventricular septal defect, and papillary muscle rupture) peak between days 3 and 7.
explanations.source_document: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 12: Diseases of the Heart; Myocardial Infarction Timeline

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Wavy myocardial fibers at borders, contraction band necrosis, and early interstitial edema are characteristic of early reperfusion or acute ischemia within the first 1 to 4 hours post-infarction, before significant leukocytic invasion.
explanations.source_document: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 12: Morphologic Evolution of Myocardial Infarction

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Dense, acellular collagenous scar tissue requires at least 2 to 3 months to develop fully after progressive remodeling of granulation tissue.
explanations.source_document: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 12: Scarring & Healing of Myocardial Infarcts

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Granulation tissue with budding neovessels and young loose fibroblastic stroma predominates between days 7 and 14 post-MI, as macrophage debridement winds down.
explanations.source_document: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 12: Granulation Phase of MI Repair

explanations.explanation_text: CORRECT: Alveolar gas equation: PAO2 = PiO2 - (PaCO2 / R) = (150 mmHg) - (62 / 0.8) = 150 - 77.5 = 72.5 mmHg. The patient's measured PaO2 is 58 mmHg. Therefore, A-a gradient = PAO2 - PaO2 = 72.5 - 58 = 14.5 mmHg (normal for age, typically < 15-20 mmHg). A normal A-a gradient in the setting of severe hypoxemia and hypercapnia conclusively demonstrates central alveolar hypoventilation (opioid respiratory depression) as the sole etiology.
explanations.source_document: West's Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials, 11th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 5: Ventilation-Perfusion Relationships; The A-a Gradient

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Pulmonary edema produces fluid-filled alveoli with true right-to-left physiologic shunt, causing an abnormally elevated A-a gradient that fails to correct with modest supplemental O2.
explanations.source_document: West's Respiratory Physiology, 11th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 5: Physiologic Shunt and Elevated A-a Gradient

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Pulmonary embolism creates dead-space ventilation and localized V/Q mismatches with compensatory tachypnea (hypocapnia, low PaCO2) and an elevated A-a gradient, whereas this patient has respiratory bradypnea and severe hypercapnia.
explanations.source_document: West's Respiratory Physiology, 11th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 5: Pulmonary Embolism & V/Q Derangements

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Under normal ambient conditions, PAO2 is always greater than or equal to PaO2; a negative A-a gradient is non-physiologic and indicates laboratory calibration error.
explanations.source_document: The explanation is not available in the provided source files.
explanations.source_reference: Unreferenced physiological constraint

explanations.explanation_text: CORRECT: Serum Anion Gap = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]) = 132 - (94 + 10) = 132 - 104 = 28 mEq/L (Normal reference is 8-12 mEq/L). In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), absolute insulin deficiency stimulates uncontrolled adipocyte lipolysis, shunting free fatty acids to hepatic beta-oxidation and ketogenesis. Accumulation of acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate anions creates a profound high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
explanations.source_document: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 53: Acid-Base Disorders; Anion Gap Acidosis

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: A calculated value of 12 mEq/L ignores the actual measured serum electrolytes: 132 - 104 = 28 mEq/L. Normal anion gap acidosis (e.g. diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis) features proportional hyperchloremia.
explanations.source_document: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 53: Normal Anion Gap (Hyperchloremic) Acidosis

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: The mathematical calculation yields 28 mEq/L, not 38 mEq/L. Furthermore, hyperchloremic saline expansion causes a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, not a widened gap.
explanations.source_document: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 53: Iatrogenic Acid-Base Derangements

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Low anion gap (<6 mEq/L) is caused by severe hypoalbuminemia (each 1 g/dL drop in albumin drops anion gap by ~2.5 mEq/L) or paraproteinemia (multiple myeloma), which is absent in this acute DKA presentation.
explanations.source_document: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 53: Low Anion Gap Determinants

explanations.explanation_text: CORRECT: Amiodarone prominently prolongs the QT interval due to IKr potassium channel blockade (Class III effect). However, it exhibits a remarkably low incidence (<1%) of Torsades de Pointes. This cardioprotective profile stems from its multi-channel blockade: by concurrently inhibiting inward L-type Ca2+ currents and late sodium currents, it suppresses the early afterdepolarizations (EADs) that trigger triggered arrhythmias and produces homogenous prolongation of ventricular repolarization without spatial dispersion.
explanations.source_document: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 29: Antiarrhythmic Drugs; Class III Amiodarone

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Procainamide is a Class Ia agent that prolongs QT and has an active metabolite (NAPA) with pure Class III properties that poses a substantial risk of Torsades de Pointes, particularly in renal dysfunction.
explanations.source_document: Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 14: Class Ia Antiarrhythmics

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Ibutilide is a potent pure Class III IV agent that causes marked transmural dispersion of repolarization, producing Torsades de Pointes in up to 4-8% of treated patients.
explanations.source_document: Katzung's Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 14: Pure Class III Agents and Proarrhythmia

explanations.explanation_text: INCORRECT: Quinidine was historically the prototypical cause of "quinidine syncope" due to marked concentration-independent prolongation of repolarization and frequent Torsades de Pointes.
explanations.source_document: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th Edition
explanations.source_reference: Chapter 29: Quinidine Syncope and Torsades
